Lloyds Scam Texts: How to Spot a Fake Lloyds SMS (UK)

Lloyds Bank will never ask for your security details via text — but scammers will try to trick you into thinking they have.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-04-23 · Updated 2026-07-26 · 5 min read

Lloyds scam textfake Lloyds text messageLloyds SMS scam
Quick answer: Lloyds may send links to its secure app or information pages, so a link alone does not prove a scam. Never use a message link to enter logon, banking or personal details or move money. Open the Lloyds app yourself, type lloydsbank.com, or dial 159, and forward a suspicious text to 7726.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What a fake Lloyds text looks like

A Lloyds scam text is smishing: a fake SMS that pretends to be from the bank so you tap a link and give away banking details, card details, or a one-time passcode. An example of the style is: LLOYDS: A new payee was added to your account. If this wasn't you, cancel here: lloyds-verify-account.example.

The hook changes - a new payee, blocked card, payment on hold, suspicious login, or account restriction - but the aim is to make you panic and tap before you verify.

Why the fake can look real

Scammers can use familiar-looking sender names and copy the tone of real bank alerts. A fake text can appear near genuine bank messages on your phone, so you cannot rely on the display name or conversation thread.

Lloyds' official fraud contact page says Lloyds Bank will never ask you to tell them account details, share your Personal Security Number, tell them your PIN or card expiry date, or move money to another account. If a text asks for any of that, treat it as a scam.

Lloyds' current scam-messages page also says it may send you links to its secure app or to pages with more information, but that it will never link directly to its Internet Banking log on page or to a page asking for your logon, banking or personal details. So the presence of a link is not the test — what the page then asks you for is.

Signs a Lloyds text is a scam

  • It rushes you: a payee "added", card "blocked", or deadline to avoid losing access.
  • It links you to "cancel", "verify", "secure", log in, or re-enter card details.
  • The link goes to a lookalike or unfamiliar domain. Do not use text-message links for banking.
  • It asks for banking details, card details, a passcode or your Personal Security Number. Lloyds says it will never ask you to share any of these, and the same goes for your log-on password, user ID or memorable information.
  • It tells you to move money to a new, holding, or "safe" account.
  • A generic greeting can be a clue, but it is weaker in SMS than email.
  • Errors can be clues, but a tidy text is not proof.

How the scam plays out

First, an unexpected text appears to come from Lloyds about a new payee, blocked payment, or login. Second, it pushes you to tap a link. Third, the link opens a copycat page that asks for banking or card details. Fourth, the criminals capture what you enter. Fifth, they may trigger a real one-time passcode and ask for it on the fake page. Finally, they try to move money, add payees, or use the details for further fraud.

Check it safely, without tapping anything

Never dial a number or open a link that the text itself supplied. Reach Lloyds by a route you chose:

  • Hang up and dial 159 yourself. Stop Scams UK says the route you reach by dialling 159 cannot be spoofed or impersonated, and 159 will never call you. Lloyds Bank is one of the participating banks.
  • Open the official Lloyds app and read your activity and secure messages there.
  • Type lloydsbank.com into the browser yourself, or use a bookmark you saved earlier.
  • Ring the number printed on the back of your Lloyds card.

Not every genuine text is mirrored as an in-app message, so silence in the app is not by itself a warning sign. If nothing independent confirms the claim, contact Lloyds directly.

If you are unsure whether a linked website is a copycat, our guide on Is This Website a Scam? A Practical Checklist Before You Buy walks through the checks.

If you tapped the link or shared details

If you entered banking details, card details, a passcode or your Personal Security Number, call 159 or the number on your card straight away and ask Lloyds to secure the account. Change your Lloyds password only inside the official app or on an address you typed yourself, and change it anywhere else you reused it.

Our scam recovery checklist takes the rest in order: stopping and reissuing the card, spotting payments, payees and account changes you did not authorise, and the money-recovery routes.

If you bank elsewhere, the same checks apply — see, for example, our Fake Halifax Text? Scam Checks, 159 and Safe Reporting guide.

How to report a Lloyds scam text (UK)

Forward the text to 7726. The NCSC says most UK phone providers let customers report suspicious texts for free this way.

If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

Tell Lloyds what happened using the app or your card number, and screenshot the message before you delete it.

Frequently asked questions

Is a Lloyds text with a link always a scam?

No. Genuine Lloyds messages can carry links, so the link alone settles nothing. Judge the request instead: never use a text link to sign in, confirm details, key in a one-time passcode, or move money.

Can a scam text appear with real Lloyds messages?

Yes. A spoofed sender ID drops the fake into the same thread as genuine alerts, so where a message sits in the thread is not evidence. Confirm it in the Lloyds app, on 159, or using your card.

What number should I call to check a Lloyds text safely?

Call 159, or the number printed on the back of your Lloyds card. Never ring a number that the suspicious text supplied — it may connect you straight to the criminals.

I tapped the link and entered my details - what now?

Contact Lloyds immediately using 159, the app, or the number on your card. Change your password through the official app or site, stop your card if needed, and report any payment you did not make.

Can I get my money back if I paid a Lloyds scammer?

Possibly. Eligible UK bank transfers over Faster Payments or CHAPS made on or after 7 October 2024 may be covered by APP reimbursement rules, subject to limits and exclusions. Card payments have different protections, such as chargeback.
